# Pathway headers encoded by this library and read back by the reference decoders of the
# official tracers. Each entry states the pathway, the base64 this library's encoder emits for
# it, and what each tracer's own decoder returned for those bytes: the decoded hash and
# timestamps, and the header that decoder re-encoded. The base64 fields are the captured
# output of those implementations, so they are a recording and not a specification: when a
# change in this library fails the comparison, the encoder moved and that is the finding.
#
# dd-trace-go v2, commit 31c447c: internal/datastreams.DecodeBase64/EncodeBase64.
# dd-trace-java 1.67.1: datadog.trace.agent.core.datastreams.DefaultPathwayContext.decode/encode.
# dd-trace-py 3.17.0: DataStreamsProcessor.decode_pathway and DataStreamsCtx.encode.
#
# Timestamps are Unix milliseconds; Java reports a start in nanoseconds and its hash as a
# signed long, so -1 is the same hash as 18446744073709551615. Java does not expose the edge
# start, which the re-encoded header covers instead.
#
# The last entry is the widest varint the format allows, timestamps of 2^56 milliseconds.
# dd-trace-py and this library read it back exactly; dd-trace-go stops early and reports
# 4611686018427 (its encoder then writes that truncated value), and dd-trace-java clamps the
# start to the largest signed long, so neither re-encodes to the same bytes. It is recorded
# rather than corrected because it is what those decoders do, and a timestamp of that
# magnitude is not a wall clock any tracer produces.
